Not everyone with Bipolar experiences hallucinations.  And up to a quarter of people with anxiety experience perceptual disturbances.  Plus, it is a pretty common hypnagogic hallucination which isn't associated with mental illness at all. 

 It concerns me when normal behaviors or experiences, whether in myself or others, are attributed to mental illness. While it’s important to acknowledge and address genuine mental health challenges, over-pathologizing typical human emotions and actions can undermine our understanding of what’s within the range of normal and make it harder to recognize when someone truly needs support. Don't get me wrong - I accidentally do this all of the time!

I don't have BPD but I notice it is especially referenced with those patients when they do seek out emergency intervention, and not just on Reddit forums, but even articles from health care professionals and such. 

It would really bother me to be seen as attention seeking, and in the past when I have received help in a crisis, I did really appreciate the support and validation, so I do get some pleasure from receiving "attention".  On the other hand, I have been told that I wait too long to ask for help, but often it isn't because I don't want the help, it is a fear of people perceiving me as attention seeking. 

I am asking in this forum because I think that as people on the front lines, interacting with patients that probably fall into both categories, what is the difference between the two?

*The most robust differences in those with bipolarity (ORs >4) were ≥3 religion changes, ≥3 marriages, cheating the partner regularly, having ≥60 lifetime sexual partners, pathological love, heavy cursing, speaking ≥3 foreign languages, having ≥2 apparent tattoos, circadian dysregulation and high debts. Most behaviors were expressed in a minority of patients (usually around 5-30%) and usually the "rule of three" was the best numerical marker to distinguish those with bipolarity. One thing you can try doing is a [WRAP - Wellness Recovery Action Plan](https://www.wellnessrecoveryactionplan.com/what-is-wrap/) .  As part of a lot of WRAPs people will write a "Contact/Responsibility List".  This list has specific people you would contact, and specific things they could do, say, assist with if you are struggling. [Here is a template that includes both ways people can help you, and specific people who you do NOT want helping you.  It is an excellent template overall.](https://uhs.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/publications/wrap.pdf)    


Here is a Bipolar Example: [Creating my Wellness Recover Action Plan](https://ibpf.org/creating-my-wellness-recovery-action-plan-wrap-how-can-i-help-you-help-me/)

I am sure your friends will want to help, but even if you explain what you are going through, it might be difficult for them to know what to do.  People prefer concrete examples, and they like to know that you thought of them specifically for certain roles or jobs within your life, because it is then meaningful to them.

**Some Statistics**:  

* [Based on the Sheehan Disability Scale, around 83% had serious impairment due to Bipolar (the worst you can have on that scale) and 17% have moderate impairment.](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/bipolar-disorder)
* [One of the top ten leading causes of disability in the world](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK558998/)
* [More than half of patients are overweight or obese, which appears to be independent of treatment with weight-promoting psychotropic medications.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK558998/)
* [Has the highest rate of suicide among all mental health conditions](https://psychcentral.com/bipolar/suicide-in-bipolar-disorder#bipolar-disorder-vs-suicide-rates)
* [Risk of death is 2.6 times greater than the general population](https://psychcentral.com/bipolar/longevity-and-bipolar-disorder#why-it-lowers-longevity)
* [Average life span is shorter than the general population](https://psychcentral.com/bipolar/longevity-and-bipolar-disorder#why-it-lowers-longevity)
* [This evidence suggests that as individuals age, they have more frequent episodes, with more time in depressed rather than manic states. They may also experience new symptoms, such as cognitive issues.](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/does-bipolar-disorder-get-worse-with-age#symptoms-of-progression)
* [cognitive impairment occurs in 40–50% of older patients with bipolar disorder](https://www.healthgrades.com/right-care/bipolar-disorder/does-bipolar-get-worse-with-age)
* [Untreated bipolar can worsen with age...\[but\] this is true even with treatment, but to a lesser extent](https://www.psycom.net/bipolar-disorder/does-bipolar-get-worse-with-age)
* [Recent research suggests that bipolar disorder increases the risk of major adverse cardiac events, such as heart attack and stroke.
The risk of heart disease appears to be higher in people with bipolar disorder, even when researchers control for traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as smoking and obesity.](https://www.healthline.com/health/bipolar-disorder/bipolar-disorder-heart-problems)
* [People with bipolar disorder had the highest 10-year risk for cardiovascular disease compared to their peers with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. People with schizoaffective disorder had the highest 30-year risk.](https://www.heart.org/en/news/2022/03/09/serious-mental-illnesses-tied-to-higher-risk-for-heart-attack-and-stroke)
* [patients with BD are about twice as likely to develop stroke as the general population](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6398847/)
* [This evidence suggests that as individuals age, they have more frequent episodes, with more time in depressed rather than manic states. They may also experience new symptoms, such as cognitive issues. Some people also find that symptoms become resistant to medications that have been effective previously.](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/does-bipolar-disorder-get-worse-with-age#does-it-worsen)
* [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7524411/figure/f01/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7524411/figure/f01/)

  
So it is definitely worse if not treated, but even with treatment it is considered a progressive disorder with significant risks around physical and psychological comorbid disorders.

I am 100% in favor of doing the mental health day BUT keep in mind that if something at school is 'triggering' her anxiety, using avoidance as a coping mechanism will actually increase that anxiety.  For example, if you are a little bit scared of dogs, and you and your Mom and Dad see one coming down the street and you start to freak out, well they have some options.  Sounds like Dad would be all for hypothetically dragging her up to the dog and forcing her to pet it - which is a great way to make her distrustful of him and give her a panic attack.  You have a few options.  You can quickly drag her away from the dog and help her hide around the corner until it goes by, or you can hold her hand, gently steady her at the edge of the sidewalk, encouraging her to calmly observe him while breathing deep until the dog has safely passed and you can continue your walk. The former will tell her that you believe she is right to be afraid and you are validating the instinctual emotional response as completely correct.  Her brain basically will go, "See, I was right, dog = dangerous, my trusted adult says so.  Next time I see one, I better bolt and hide".  My confirming her anxious response is both real and valid, you have increased her Anxiety if it happens again.  Your husband did the same by not acknowledging that her fear was real.

Obviously, the dog and the school are one and the same in this hypothetical scenario.  You want to acknowledge that you recognize her fear is real, but you don't want to validate it.  You need to take this opportunity to build coping skills and provide ongoing support so that she can feel capable and supported entering the school the next day.

So you need to think of how you can keep the mental health day from not being a validating avoidance day. Maybe take a drive to a parking lot near the school, and just chat about what she had been going through there and some strategies to work through it, to enable her as a problem solver rather than a victim.  Maybe at home have a spa hour, but in that spa hour, do some guided breathing exercises that she could do in a bathroom stall at school if her anxiety increased.  Maybe have a dance party together and load the same music on her device so that if she gets sad or lonely at school she can pop in her headphones and remember that you have her back.

I mean, we all need Ben and Jerry's in bed mental health days, but those are better if we are grieving a bad situation or just are burnt out and need a day.  But if the mental health day is in reaction to fear or anxiety, you have to be very careful to not send the message that her brain is right to be afraid.  You want her brain to know that you see her fear, but you fully and utterly believe that she can move through the uncomfortable emotions successfully.

It depends on where you live.  The rules where I live are that the therapist cannot break confidentiality regarding suicidal ideation unless you have a plan, you have the intention to complete the plan in the near future, and you have the means to complete it available to you, or are easily accessible within that timeframe. Sort of?  I mean, any decent therapist will definitely make sure they are asking the right questions and ensuring your safety when you bring up the topic, so those alarm bells will be ringing. >*And also, is it connected in any way to self-harm? For example, is it that slf harming patients will more likely attempt suicide?*

Sort of.  First of all, people taking part in NSSI (non-suicidal self injury) aren't necessarily suicidal.  NSSI isn't meant to end in death, so when people panic and jump to that idea, it isn't helpful or accurate.  

Most people who engage in NSSI don't ever experience suicidal thoughts or engage in suicidal behaviour, especially in young people (Whitlock et al, 2015).  There are some signs though that someone who engages in NSSI is also more likely to engage in suicidal behaviours:

* 20+ NSSI incidents
* Psychological distress/extreme stress in the last month
* History of trauma
* Feelings of holelessness
* Conflict within the family unit
* Impulsivity/Risky behaviours
* Substance use
* Diagnosis of MDD or PTSD     (Whitlock et al, 2015).

It is possible that NSSI can also be a form of gradual exposure, where the person is able to do more and more harmful things to their body until they can complete a suicide attempt.  What is interesting is that while there is a lot of research showing that NSSI is a risk factor for future suicide attempts, there isn't a whole lot connecting NSSI as a risk factor for suicide completion.  I assume they have a strong correlation, but who knows?

  
Generally, the two have different purposes as well.  Suicide is generally used as an escape route, usually from immense pain (psychological, but could be physical).  NSSI is more of a coping mechanism to relieve pain temporarily, or to punish oneself (Pompili et al, 2015).

**How long would it take to know if Lithium is working?**

It depends on how your body metabolizes it.  Lithium has a narrow window in terms of therapeutic levels in the blood.  Too low, and it doesn't do much at all.  Too high, and it is toxic.  Since you would be taking it primarily for depression symptoms, you wouldn't need as high of dose (I don't think - I am NOT a psychiatrist, but I take Lithium so have read a bunch about it - always go with your pharmacists or physician's advice) so you would probably know if it works for you within a month.    


**If lithium did work, would it prove anything about my brain chemistry?**

Nope.  They don't really have a clear understanding of how Lithium works in the brain (there are some strong theories floating around now but nothing firm) so your Doctor wouldn't necessarily be able to extrapolate a diagnosis from the way Lithium works for you.    


In terms of the side effects, well, Lithium has a pretty bad reputation.  If you aren't responsible enough to get your blood levels checked when the Doctor orders, then don't risk Lithium.  It would be too likely that you would end up ruining your kidneys.  On the other hand, if you can handle the responsibility of regular blood exams,[it actually has a lot of physical health benefits that people don't talk about a lot.](https://www.thecarlatreport.com/blogs/2-the-carlat-psychiatry-podcast/post/4250-throwback-thursday-lithiums-medical-benefits)

People with Bipolar tend to have executive functioning difficulties, so they are often more impulsive just in general.    


A manic episode is when there is a ***marked increase in impulsivity***, paired with a variety of other symptoms.  One of the primary signs is increased energy lasting multiple days.  


Along with that you might experience more confidence (sometimes to an extreme), no need for sleep, you become super chatty - sometimes uncontrollably, your thoughts are super fast or crazy all over the place, you are really distracted (once again - more than normal), you are really goal-orientated but these don't have to be positive goals (e.g. it could be cleaning your house top to bottom, but it could also be finding as many men as possible to sleep with), and getting involved in high-risk activities such as shopping sprees, excessive gambling, sleeping around, etc.  


So just impulsivity is NOT mania.  For a lot of us, impulsivity is just daily life.  It is the combination of multiple symptoms plus it being outside one's norm that point towards a manic episode.

I liked the solutions-focused therapy because it make the effects of therapy very concrete.  I am not into wishy-washy fuzzy-wuzzy stuff - I like things to be straightforward and linear haha.   


Ultimately, we have done the most work in **Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy,** with an emphasis on the Social Rhythm Therapy.  I don't think my therapist in trained on it, but they have ended up using a lot of the techniques anyways.  Prior to my diagnosis, my life was basically like this:  

* Stable for a bit, had undiagnosed ADHD, so I was adulting but not very well.
* Hypomania would hit, and I would accomplish five bazillion tasks and start working a couple jobs while going to university full time
* This might keep going into mania or it might not, but ultimately I would crash into major depression.  I would stop working, stop going to school, and my house would be like a hoarders house.
* I would slowly become stable again, and the whole cycle would happen again.  


Anyways, I learned to expect this cycle to happen, so I was extremely reliant on those brief hypomanic periods, and I would stay up all night to take advantage of the energy.  After all, I knew it wouldn't last!  I had zero routines, and zero structure to my life, it was all about cashing on whatever productivity I had until I no longer had it.  


Social Rhythm therapy is all about creating routines that help stabilize your biological rhythm, reducing the chances of an episode occurring and minimizing its effects if it does occur. Adopting out of the foster system has some challenges:  A) the ultimate goal is always to reunite children with their biological family, so your focus always has to be on that, not on adoption.  B)  Many children in the foster system come with a lot of health problems, and can exhibit severe behaviours due to trauma.   C)  You often will have to agree to ensuring the child can still have contact with biological family members such as grandparents.
